Anthropic privately pitched lawmakers its own draft bill on frontier AI safety, Politico reported.
The government could block a model only for an imminent risk of over $1 billion in damage or harm to more than 50 people.
Paid outside evaluators would report risks to the Commerce Department within 72 hours.

slides.heading: A bill *written by Anthropic*
paras: Anthropic representatives privately pitched a draft bill on frontier AI safety to lawmakers on Capitol Hill, Politico reported Friday, citing three people familiar with the effort.
An Anthropic spokesperson said the bill reflects ideas from the company's Advanced AI Framework, released earlier this year.

slides.heading: The *$1 billion* line
paras: The government could block a model's release or use only for a foreseeable, imminent risk of over $1 billion in damage, or of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people.
That risk would have to come from a biological weapon, a cyberattack or a model evading its developer's controls.

slides.heading: Paid testers, *72 hour* alarm
paras: Labs would have to test frontier models, disclose findings and get independent evaluations. Evaluators would register with the Commerce Department, and labs could pay them, but not based on results.
If an evaluator finds an imminent risk, it must notify Commerce within 72 hours of finishing its assessment.

slides.heading: One judge holds *the brake*
paras: Only Commerce could ask a court to halt a model, and only a federal judge in Washington, D.C., could order a suspension.

paras.t: No other federal agency could pause a model's development, deployment or internal use on its own.

slides.hook: AI labs are now drafting the rules for their own models. Follow to see if Congress signs on.
